newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Commonwealth officials push for Nigeria probe.
newsitem.headline: Commonwealth officials push for Nigeria probe.

text.p: Four Commonwealth officials arrived in Nigeria on Monday to press its military government to allow a probe of human rights and democracy.

The team led by Commonwealth Deputy Secretary-General Srina Vasan, a former Indian ambassador to Nigeria and deputy Indian foreign minister, arrived in the capital, Abuja, in the morning, foreign ministry officials said.
An official said he knew of no plan for them to see Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi during the visit, which is expected to last two days.

Commonwealth ministers, meeting in London last month, agreed to send the officials to pave the way for a ministerial level mission, after a proposed visit was called off when Nigeria imposed strict conditions.
The Commonwealth, concerned about human rights, wants to send a fact-finding team that would meet people outside the government, including the opposition and political prisoners.
But Abuja says the only question on the agenda is Nigeria's suspension from the Commonwealth last November over human rights concerns.
Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi recently told Reuters Nigeria had no objection to the visit of the officials but he did not have plans to meet them.
"At this stage I can say I have not heard of a plan for them to meet the foreign minister," a foreign ministry official said on Monday.

Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation was suspended from the 53-member Commonwealth of Britain and its former colonies in November after the execution of author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other minority rights activists on murder charges.
A Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG) was set up in the wake of the hangings, which triggered worldwide condemnation of Nigeria's military government.

CMAG agreed in May to impose sanctions to push Nigeria toward democracy, including a ban on sporting links and arms sales. But at a meeting in London in June, CMAG said the measures would be suspended until a New York meeting in September to give Nigeria a chance for further talks.
Only Canada said it would go it alone and impose its own sanctions. It is pushing for other Commonwealth countries to take a harder line.
Nigeria on Friday said it was closing its embassy in Canada because of economic constraints.
Military ruler General Sani Abacha last year set out a plan to restore civilian rule by October 1998, which critics at home and abroad say allows too much time.
The last attempt to end army rule collapsed in 1993, when a previous military government annulled elections and plunged Nigeria into political crisis.
